$comment: Conformance cases for the contributed-command contract, consumed by BOTH validators:
It exists because the two rulebooks are written twice, in two languages, and were
mirrored only by comment -- which failed twice in review on the branch that added
them: the title cap and the per-app command cap each shipped on one side only, and
both had the same consequence (a manifest that installs clean, then loses rows in
the launcher with no error its author can see). A comment cannot fail a build.
Each case is a WHOLE `contributes` block plus whether the contract accepts it.
`accept: false` means the command does not reach the launcher -- refused by the
manifest, skipped by the frontend, or both. The two sides report differently (a
list of errors vs a console warning and a dropped row), so each harness asserts in
its own idiom; what this file pins is the VERDICT, which must agree.
`commands` counts how many survive, so a case can pin partial acceptance -- one bad
entry dropped while its siblings load.
Add a case here FIRST when adding a kind, a cap or a refusal. A rule with no case
is a rule that exists on one side.

cases.name: a minimal well-formed command
a url argument with a host allowlist
a text argument
an argument with no kind defaults to text
exactly the per-app command cap
a title exactly at the cap
an id that is not a kebab slug
a missing title
a missing prompt
a prompt that interpolates but declares no argument
an argument the prompt never interpolates
autoSend with no argument, so no preview can be shown

why: The one DELIBERATE difference between the two validators, spelled out here so
neither side is later 'fixed' into matching the other by mistake.
The manifest REFUSES it: an app author who wrote this believes their command
auto-sends, and it never will, so silence would leave them debugging a row
that works but does nothing they asked for.
The frontend KEEPS the row and clamps autoSend off. It has to: an unknown
manifest key reaches the dashboard through `extra` having passed no schema, so
the frontend sees manifests the validator never saw. Dropping the row would
remove a command that is perfectly usable as a prefill; clamping keeps it and
removes only the capability that had no consent path.

cases.name: an argument still carrying the retired pattern key
an unknown argument kind
hosts on a kind with no notion of them
an argument value that is not an object
$why: The prompt deliberately does NOT interpolate: with a token present, the older
'interpolates but declares no argument' error already rejects this, so the case
would pass whether or not the non-object shape is caught. Without the token,
nothing else fires -- this is the input that installed clean and then rendered
no row, because the frontend tells 'no argument' apart from 'argument broken'.

cases.name: a commands value that is not an array
$why: The frontend already refused this; the manifest coerced it to an empty list, so
the declaration passed validation and then vanished from to_dict -- no error and
no rows. Same fail-open shape as a non-array hosts.

cases.name: a hosts value that is not an array
$why: Coercing a non-array to [] does not mean 'no opinion' -- an empty allowlist
means ANY host, so the restriction the author wrote would be erased silently
while autoSend stayed on. Both validators must refuse it, not normalize it.

cases.name: exactly the keyword cap
one past the keyword cap

why: Same shape as the autoSend case: the manifest tells the author, the frontend
keeps the row. A keyword is ADDITIVE by definition -- dropping the overflow
costs a match the reader probably was not typing, while dropping the row costs
them the command itself. The frontend also sees manifests that never passed the
validator (the `extra` path), so it cannot assume the count was checked.
The bound exists at all because ranking walks every keyword on every keystroke.

cases.name: a keyword exactly at the length cap
a keyword one past the length cap

why: The same asymmetry as the keyword COUNT case, and it belongs here for the
reason this file's header gives: a rule with no case is a rule that exists on
one side. Review found it missing, which is the fixture working as intended --
the gap was in the cases, not in the code.
Manifest refuses so the author is told. Frontend filters the offending alias and
keeps the row, because a keyword is additive: losing one costs a match, losing
the row costs the command.
Review also proposed deleting the manifest refusal instead, on the grounds that
the per-keystroke cost is a frontend cost the frontend already bounds. Kept
deliberately: without it a manifest with 500-character aliases installs clean
and is silently trimmed, which is the 'passes install, then degrades with no
error the author ever sees' shape that this same review made us fix for the
title and command-count caps. The refusal is what makes the trim visible.

cases.name: a host entry that is not a hostname
duplicate ids
an argument hint longer than the title cap
$why: hint, placeholder and patternError were the last app-supplied strings with no
bound on either side. They are not searched, so they cost layout rather than
per-keystroke work -- an outsized one pushes the resolved-prompt preview and the
footer around, and that preview is the consent surface for autoSend.

cases.name: a subtitle longer than the title cap
$why: The subtitle is SEARCHED -- rankRootRows runs fuzzyMatch over it on every
keystroke -- so it belongs with the title and keyword bounds. It was the last
searchable string left unbounded on either side, which made the other caps
incomplete rather than wrong.

cases.name: a non-object entry beside a good one
$why: Same split as the bad-id case, and deliberate: the manifest REFUSES so the app
author is told an entry vanished, while the launcher keeps the good rows so one
typo cannot empty the array at runtime. Before this the manifest filtered the
entry out silently and validated clean -- five declared commands could install
as four with no warning.

cases.name: one bad entry does not take its siblings down
one past the per-app command cap
a title one past the cap
a prompt one past the cap
a host allowlist one past the cap
